raw.title: Dow Jones Industrial Average reaches intra-year peak
raw.description: The Dow reached its highest level of the early-2000 period before the broader market deterioration set in, reflecting residual strength in blue-chip and ‘old-economy’ names even as technology leadership was already fracturing.
raw.middle_circle: Many expected the Dow to continue higher in parallel with the Nasdaq; the subsequent divergence became a defining feature of 2000.
raw.outer_circle: The Dow proved far more resilient than the Nasdaq over the full year, finishing down only about 6% versus the Nasdaq’s 39% decline, highlighting the extreme sector concentration of the bubble.
sources: Historical price data and contemporaneous reports
raw.notes: Useful reference high for the non-tech portion of the market.

raw.title: Federal Reserve raises federal funds rate 25 bp to 5.75%
raw.description: The FOMC increased the target federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.75%, continuing the tightening cycle begun in 1999 amid strong growth and tight labour markets.
raw.middle_circle: A hike was widely anticipated; debate centred on whether the Fed would signal a more aggressive path or remain measured.
raw.outer_circle: Equities absorbed the move with limited immediate damage, but the cumulative effect of tightening contributed to the later revaluation of high-growth stocks.
raw.notes: First rate increase of 2000.

raw.title: Crude oil reaches nine-year high above $34
raw.description: NYMEX WTI closed at $34.13, the highest level in nine years, reflecting tight inventories, strong demand and limited OPEC spare capacity.
raw.middle_circle: Further upside was expected by some, but many still anticipated that OPEC would respond with additional supply.
raw.outer_circle: Energy equities rallied while inflation-sensitive assets came under pressure. The move set the stage for the even higher prices reached later in the year.
raw.notes: Early marker of the 2000 oil-price spike.

raw.title: Nasdaq Composite peaks and begins multi-year collapse
raw.description: The Nasdaq Composite closed at its all-time high of 5048.62, marking the top of the dot-com bubble. Over the following two years the index lost ~78% as internet valuations collapsed amid rising rates and earnings disappointments.
raw.middle_circle: Many analysts and momentum strategies still projected continued 'new economy' outperformance; valuation metrics were widely dismissed as obsolete.
raw.outer_circle: Volume and breadth deteriorated sharply; subsequent price action showed order-flow rotation out of growth into value and cash far faster and deeper than most quantitative models had projected from 1999 positioning data.
raw.notes: US tech/microstructure gap-filler. Exact contemporaneous OI limited; peak-to-trough volume and subsequent drawdown used.

raw.title: Nasdaq Composite reaches all-time peak of 5048.62
raw.description: The Nasdaq Composite closed at its historic high of 5,048.62, marking the climax of the late-1990s technology and internet bubble after more than doubling in the previous twelve months.
raw.middle_circle: Momentum investors and many strategists still expected further gains driven by the ‘new economy’; traditional valuation concerns were widely dismissed.
raw.outer_circle: The peak proved to be the definitive top. Within weeks the index entered a rapid decline that would eventually erase more than 50% of its value by year-end and far more by 2002.
raw.notes: Canonical start date of the dot-com bear market.

raw.title: Federal Reserve raises federal funds rate 25 bp to 6.00%
raw.description: The FOMC raised the federal funds target another 25 basis points to 6.00% as part of its campaign to cool an overheating economy and contain inflation risks.
raw.middle_circle: Further tightening was expected; markets were increasingly sensitive to the cumulative impact on equity valuations.
raw.outer_circle: Technology stocks continued to weaken in the weeks following the decision, accelerating the rotation out of high-multiple growth names.
raw.notes: Second hike of 2000.

raw.location_name: Washington, D.C. / New York, United States
raw.title: Microsoft settlement talks collapse; Nasdaq records large decline
raw.description: Settlement negotiations between Microsoft and the Department of Justice broke down. Judge Jackson prepared to issue his final liability ruling. The Nasdaq fell more than 7% on the day, one of its largest point declines to that date.
raw.middle_circle: A settlement had been hoped for by many investors; the failure raised the probability of severe structural remedies.
raw.outer_circle: Microsoft shares plunged and the broader technology complex sold off sharply. The episode reinforced the shift in sentiment against high-valuation tech names.
raw.notes: Key catalyst in the early phase of the Nasdaq decline.

raw.title: Nasdaq falls more than 25% from March peak
raw.description: Within roughly five weeks of its March 10 high the Nasdaq Composite had declined more than 25%, entering official bear-market territory at unprecedented speed for a major U.S. index.
raw.middle_circle: Many still viewed the decline as a healthy correction within a secular bull market; the speed of the drop exceeded most risk models.
raw.outer_circle: Forced selling, margin calls and a collapse in IPO activity amplified the move. The rapidity of the bear market became a defining feature of the 2000–2002 tech crash.
raw.notes: Milestone confirming the end of the late-1990s bubble phase.

raw.title: Federal Reserve raises federal funds rate 50 bp to 6.50%
raw.description: In its most aggressive move of the cycle, the FOMC raised the federal funds target by 50 basis points to 6.50%, the highest level of the expansion, citing strong demand and elevated resource utilisation.
raw.middle_circle: A 50 bp move had been increasingly priced after strong data; some still expected only 25 bp.
raw.outer_circle: Equities weakened further. The hike marked the peak of the tightening cycle; rates remained at 6.50% for the rest of 2000 before the eventual easing that began in 2001.
raw.notes: Final and largest rate increase of the 1999–2000 tightening cycle.

raw.title: Boo.com collapses
raw.description: The high-profile online fashion retailer Boo.com ceased operations after burning through approximately $135 million in venture capital in 18 months, becoming one of the most visible corporate failures of the dot-com era.
raw.middle_circle: Many still believed that well-capitalised internet retailers could survive; Boo’s failure highlighted the fragility of pure-play e-commerce models with high burn rates.
raw.outer_circle: The collapse reinforced negative sentiment toward unprofitable internet companies and contributed to the broader de-rating of the sector.
raw.notes: Symbolic corporate casualty of the bubble.

raw.title: Judge Jackson orders Microsoft breakup
raw.description: U.S. District Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson issued his remedy order requiring Microsoft to be split into two separate companies—one for the Windows operating system and one for applications and other businesses—along with a series of conduct restrictions.
raw.middle_circle: A structural remedy had been widely expected after the liability findings; the precise form and severity were still debated.
raw.outer_circle: Microsoft shares rose on the day and in after-hours trading as investors concluded the worst-case outcome was already discounted and that an appeal would delay any actual breakup. The broader market also firmed.
raw.notes: Order later stayed and ultimately overturned on appeal in 2001.

raw.title: OPEC agrees to raise production quotas
raw.description: OPEC ministers agreed to increase production quotas by 708,000 barrels per day effective 1 July, taking the group’s target (excluding Iraq) to 25.4 million b/d in an attempt to moderate prices.
raw.middle_circle: Markets expected a supply response; the size and credibility of compliance remained open questions.
raw.outer_circle: Oil prices initially rose rather than fell, reflecting scepticism about the adequacy of the increase and continued strong demand. Prices remained elevated through the summer.
raw.notes: One of several OPEC adjustments during the 2000 price spike.

raw.title: Federal Reserve holds rates; balance of risks still toward inflation
raw.description: The FOMC left the federal funds rate unchanged at 6.50% but maintained a statement bias indicating that the risks remained weighted toward higher inflation.
raw.middle_circle: Markets watched closely for any shift in language that might signal the end of the tightening cycle.
raw.outer_circle: The continued inflation bias kept rate-cut expectations in check even as growth was clearly decelerating, contributing to the difficult environment for equities in the second half of the year.
raw.notes: Intermediate communication during the on-hold phase.

raw.title: Wave of technology earnings warnings begins
raw.description: A growing number of U.S. technology and telecommunications companies began issuing warnings that they would miss analyst earnings estimates, signalling a sharp slowdown in capital spending and demand after the bubble peak.
raw.middle_circle: Many investors had expected a soft landing or continued strong growth; the breadth of the warning season surprised the market.
raw.outer_circle: The Nasdaq entered a second, steeper leg of its decline that lasted into 2001. The shift from valuation compression to actual earnings disappointment marked a new phase of the bear market.
raw.notes: Fundamental catalyst for the autumn 2000 acceleration of the tech sell-off.

raw.title: Crude oil hits 10-year high near $37–38 per barrel
raw.description: NYMEX crude oil futures reached levels not seen since the 1990–91 Gulf crisis, driven by strong demand, limited OPEC spare capacity and geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.
raw.middle_circle: OPEC production increases had been expected to cap prices; the market’s willingness to push through previous highs surprised many participants.
raw.outer_circle: Energy stocks outperformed while rate-sensitive and consumer sectors faced pressure from higher input costs. The spike contributed to global inflation concerns and later policy responses including the U.S. SPR release.
raw.notes: Peak of the 2000 oil-price spike.

raw.title: G7 central banks intervene to support the euro
raw.description: At the initiative of the ECB, the Federal Reserve, Bank of Japan, Bank of England and Bank of Canada joined in a coordinated purchase of euros against their respective currencies. The euro had fallen nearly 30% from its 1999 launch level.
raw.middle_circle: Unilateral ECB action had been expected by some; full G7 participation, especially by the United States, was a genuine surprise.
raw.outer_circle: The euro jumped several cents immediately after the announcement but the gains proved temporary. The intervention highlighted the depth of concern over the currency’s weakness and its potential inflationary consequences for the euro area.
raw.notes: First major coordinated G7 FX intervention since 1998 and the first ever in support of the euro.

raw.title: United States announces release of oil from Strategic Petroleum Reserve
raw.description: The Clinton administration authorised the release of 30 million barrels from the SPR in a swap arrangement aimed at easing heating-oil and crude prices ahead of winter.
raw.middle_circle: Political motivation was widely discussed; the market impact of a relatively modest volume was debated.
raw.outer_circle: Oil prices fell several dollars in the immediate aftermath. The move was criticised by some as election-year politics but succeeded in temporarily relieving price pressure.
raw.notes: First major SPR release since the Gulf War.

raw.title: Second Intifada begins; Tel Aviv equities sell off sharply
raw.description: The outbreak of the Second Intifada triggered an immediate and sustained risk-off move on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange. The TA-100 fell ~18% in the first month and ultimately declined more than 40% peak-to-trough through early 2003 amid rising security costs, tourism collapse and concurrent global tech weakness.
raw.middle_circle: Markets had priced a manageable security deterioration after Camp David; a multi-year high-intensity conflict with large GDP and equity impact was outside the base case.
raw.outer_circle: Equity volume spiked on downside days, the shekel weakened, and the sustained drawdown exceeded the short-lived corrections typical of prior security incidents.
raw.notes: Israel-specific security shock with clear equity and tourism footprint. Equity volume and peak-to-trough move used as proxies.

raw.title: Second Intifada begins after Ariel Sharon visit to Temple Mount
raw.description: Widespread Palestinian–Israeli violence erupted following Ariel Sharon’s visit to the Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif compound, marking the start of the Second Intifada. Casualties and closures rapidly escalated.
raw.middle_circle: Markets had grown accustomed to intermittent Middle East tension; a sustained uprising of this intensity was not the base-case expectation.
raw.outer_circle: Oil prices spiked on supply-disruption fears. Israeli assets sold off and regional risk premia rose. The conflict contributed to elevated energy-price volatility through the remainder of 2000.
raw.notes: Geopolitical catalyst that reinforced the already elevated oil-price environment.

raw.title: Federal Reserve holds rates steady at 6.50%
raw.description: After the aggressive May hike, the FOMC left the federal funds rate unchanged, signalling that the cumulative tightening was being allowed to work through the economy while remaining vigilant on inflation.
raw.middle_circle: Markets debated whether the Fed had finished tightening or would still need to act again before year-end.
raw.outer_circle: The pause was interpreted as confirmation that the peak of the cycle had been reached. Equity markets remained under pressure from earnings warnings rather than from further rate fears.
raw.notes: Policy on hold for the remainder of 2000.

raw.title: USS Cole bombing in Aden harbour
raw.description: A suicide attack by al-Qaeda operatives against the U.S. Navy destroyer USS Cole killed 17 American sailors and wounded dozens more while the ship was refuelling in Aden, Yemen.
raw.middle_circle: Terrorist attacks on U.S. military assets had occurred previously, but the scale and location raised fresh concerns about broader Middle East and energy-security risks.
raw.outer_circle: Oil prices rose sharply on the day. Equity markets weakened and safe-haven flows into the dollar and Treasuries increased temporarily.
raw.notes: Early major al-Qaeda operation against a U.S. target; market impact primarily via oil and risk sentiment.

raw.title: Chevron agrees to acquire Texaco
raw.description: Chevron announced a $35.1 billion all-stock acquisition of Texaco, continuing the wave of mega-mergers in the global oil industry that had begun with BP-Amoco and Exxon-Mobil.
raw.middle_circle: Further consolidation was expected; antitrust scrutiny, particularly regarding U.S. West Coast refining and marketing, was anticipated.
raw.outer_circle: Both shares reacted positively to synergy expectations. The deal faced intensive regulatory review but ultimately closed, creating one of the largest integrated oil companies.
raw.notes: Part of the late-1990s/early-2000s oil-industry consolidation wave.

raw.title: U.S. presidential election ends in Florida recount deadlock
raw.description: The presidential contest between George W. Bush and Al Gore became deadlocked on the outcome in Florida, whose 25 electoral votes would decide the election. Networks initially called the state for Gore, then for Bush, then declared it too close to call.
raw.middle_circle: Most participants expected a clear result on election night or shortly thereafter; a multi-week constitutional and legal crisis was outside consensus forecasts.
raw.outer_circle: Equity futures and cash markets swung violently with each shift in the projected Florida result. Uncertainty persisted for 36 days until the Supreme Court decision, contributing to elevated volatility and a temporary risk-off tone.
raw.notes: Longest unresolved U.S. presidential election outcome in modern history.

raw.title: Federal Reserve maintains 6.50% funds rate amid election uncertainty
raw.description: The FOMC kept policy unchanged while the presidential election recount continued, focusing on incoming data rather than political developments.
raw.middle_circle: Some had speculated that political uncertainty might influence the Fed’s communication; the Committee remained data-driven.
raw.outer_circle: Markets continued to be dominated by technology earnings warnings and election noise rather than by monetary-policy surprises.
raw.notes: Routine hold during a period of elevated political risk.

raw.title: Nasdaq records one of its largest single-day percentage gains
raw.description: In the midst of its worst calendar year on record, the Nasdaq Composite staged a 10.5% single-day rally on 5 December, one of the largest percentage advances in its history, as short-covering and bargain-hunting temporarily overwhelmed sellers.
raw.middle_circle: Volatility was expected to remain elevated; such extreme upside days were still rare outside of crisis recoveries.
raw.outer_circle: The rally proved short-lived. The index finished the year down approximately 39%, its worst annual performance, illustrating the violent two-way price action that characterised the early bear market.
raw.notes: Illustrates the extreme volatility of 2000 technology markets.

raw.title: U.S. Supreme Court issues Bush v. Gore decision
raw.description: The Supreme Court ruled 5–4 to halt the Florida recount, effectively awarding the state’s electoral votes and the presidency to George W. Bush. Al Gore conceded the following day.
raw.middle_circle: Markets had partially priced a Bush victory but still assigned meaningful probability to a continued legal battle or a Gore win under certain recount scenarios.
raw.outer_circle: Uncertainty premium declined. Some sectors associated with Republican policy preferences outperformed in subsequent sessions, while the broader market stabilised relative to the extreme volatility of the recount period.
raw.notes: Resolved the 36-day electoral crisis.

raw.title: FTC approves AOL-Time Warner merger with conditions
raw.description: The Federal Trade Commission approved the AOL-Time Warner combination subject to strict open-access and non-discrimination conditions designed to protect competition in broadband and interactive television.
raw.middle_circle: Approval had been expected after lengthy negotiations; the severity of the conditions was the main uncertainty.
raw.outer_circle: Shares of both companies rose on the news that the last major U.S. regulatory hurdle had been cleared. The deal closed shortly thereafter, although the combined entity later destroyed substantial shareholder value.
raw.notes: Final major regulatory clearance for the iconic bubble-era merger.

raw.title: Federal Reserve holds rates at final meeting of 2000
raw.description: The FOMC left the federal funds rate at 6.50% at its last meeting of the year, with the economy showing clear signs of slowing but inflation still a residual concern.
raw.middle_circle: Growing numbers of economists expected easing to begin in early 2001; a hold was the consensus outcome for December.
raw.outer_circle: The decision was fully priced. Attention shifted to the incoming Bush administration and the likelihood of rate cuts in the new year.
raw.notes: Final policy decision before the aggressive easing cycle of 2001.

raw.title: Nasdaq plunges over 7% on first trading day of 2001
raw.description: The Nasdaq Composite fell 7.2% on the first trading session of the year amid intensifying concerns over slowing economic growth and corporate profits, particularly in technology. The index closed at 2,291.86, its worst one-day percentage decline since April 2000. Blue-chip indices also declined as investors priced in rising recession risks.
raw.middle_circle: Analysts expected continued volatility from the ongoing tech correction and soft manufacturing data, with some forecasting further declines if recession signals strengthened, while others hoped for stabilization after 2000 losses.
raw.outer_circle: Heavy selling hit technology leaders such as Cisco; bond markets rallied on safe-haven flows as the ISM manufacturing index confirmed weakness. Trading volume was elevated as the growth-to-value rotation accelerated.
raw.notes: Exact open/close timestamps approximate; event reflects cumulative year-end 2000 momentum into the new year.

raw.title: Federal Reserve emergency 50 bp rate cut to 6%
raw.description: In an unscheduled inter-meeting move, the FOMC lowered the federal funds target by 50 basis points to 6% and the discount rate by 25 bp, citing weakening sales, production, consumer confidence, and high energy prices. The action was the first rate cut since 1998 and surprised markets.
raw.middle_circle: Most analysts expected the Fed to wait until the scheduled late-January meeting and cut by only 25 bp if at all; consensus viewed the economy as slowing but not requiring emergency action.
raw.outer_circle: Nasdaq surged a record 14.2% on the day with massive volume; technology and growth stocks led a broad rally as markets priced in further easing and improved earnings outlook. Treasury yields fell sharply.
raw.notes: Announcement timing approximated from contemporary reports of early afternoon ET release.

raw.title: OPEC agrees 1.5 million bpd production cut

raw.outer_circle: Crude prices initially softened after the announcement as the decision was anticipated and Iraq export uncertainty remained; longer-term support for the $22–28 OPEC basket target was reinforced.
raw.notes: Exact announcement hour approximate; Iraq exempt from the quota cut.

raw.title: Gujarat earthquake (Mw 7.7)
raw.description: A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck western Gujarat on Republic Day, killing more than 20,000 people and causing extensive damage to infrastructure, housing and industry in Kutch district. Direct economic losses were estimated in the billions of dollars.
raw.middle_circle: Initial fears focused on disruption to Gujarat’s significant share of Indian refining, petrochemicals, textiles and ports, potentially weighing on national GDP and gold demand (Gujarat a major import hub).
raw.outer_circle: Indian equities fell on the subsequent trading day then recovered quickly as industrial facilities proved largely intact and reconstruction aid expectations rose; gold demand concerns were noted but price impact was limited.
raw.notes: National GDP impact ultimately assessed as small (<0.25% of GSDP annually); local devastation far larger.

raw.outer_circle: Utility shares remained under pressure; the blackouts intensified political pressure for state intervention and later investigations into trading practices by Enron and others.

raw.outer_circle: PCG shares were halted then plunged; related utility and energy-trading stocks sold off. The event intensified scrutiny of California deregulation and Enron’s role in the crisis.
raw.notes: Filing occurred during market hours; exact minute approximate.

raw.title: September 11 terrorist attacks on World Trade Center and Pentagon
raw.description: Four coordinated al-Qaeda hijackings struck the World Trade Center twin towers in New York and the Pentagon; a fourth aircraft crashed in Pennsylvania. Nearly 3,000 people were killed. U.S. equity markets did not open and remained closed until 17 September—the longest shutdown since the 1930s.
raw.middle_circle: No prior market pricing of a mass-casualty domestic terrorist attack of this scale; geopolitical risk was elevated after earlier al-Qaeda actions but not at this magnitude.
raw.outer_circle: Global markets that were open sold off sharply; when U.S. markets reopened, the Dow fell 7.1% on the first day and 14% over the week. Airlines, insurers and leisure stocks collapsed; defense and gold rose. Flight-to-quality flows compressed Treasury yields.
raw.notes: Timestamp is first aircraft impact (American Airlines 11 into North Tower); markets closed for the remainder of the week.

raw.title: September 11 attacks close US equity markets for four days
raw.description: Terrorist attacks destroyed the World Trade Center and damaged the Pentagon. US equity markets remained closed until 17 September—the longest halt since 1933. Upon reopening the Dow fell ~7% in a single session amid extreme volume.
raw.middle_circle: Pre-attack consensus focused on mild recession risks from the dot-com bust; geopolitical shock of this magnitude was outside most risk models.
raw.outer_circle: Flight-to-quality intensified (Treasuries and gold surged), equity volume on reopening was record-setting, and the Fed injected massive liquidity; realised volatility and order-flow disruption exceeded any 1990s stress scenario.
raw.notes: Primary US location and market-microstructure event. Exact pre-attack positioning hard to recover; reopening volume and drawdown used as proxy.

raw.description: Fighting erupted after Hezbollah captured two Israeli soldiers; Israel launched a major military offensive against Lebanon including air strikes, a naval blockade and ground operations. The conflict lasted until a UN-brokered ceasefire on 14 August.
raw.middle_circle: Markets expected a limited regional conflict with a moderate risk premium in oil; fears of wider escalation involving Syria or Iran were the main concern.
raw.outer_circle: Oil prices surged to new nominal records (Brent briefly above $78, WTI near $77). Equities sold off globally on the combination of geopolitical risk and energy-price inflation fears. Gold and safe-haven assets gained. The conflict contributed to the summer peak in oil prices.
sources: Contemporary Reuters, Times and Washington Post reports
raw.notes: Primary geopolitical driver of the mid-2006 oil-price spike.

raw.title: Israel–Hezbollah war begins; oil and regional risk premium rise
raw.description: Cross-border fighting escalated into a full-scale conflict lasting into August. Oil prices spiked toward then-record levels on supply-disruption fears while Israeli equities and the shekel experienced short-lived but sharp risk-off moves.
raw.middle_circle: Markets expected a contained border incident; a multi-week war with material oil-price impact was not the base case.
raw.outer_circle: Oil jumped several dollars per barrel in the opening days and Israeli risk assets sold off more than typical short-security events before stabilising once the conflict’s limited duration became clearer.
raw.notes: Israel-driven regional security event with commodity spill-over. Oil and equity price reaction used as proxies.

raw.location_name: Lebanon / northern Israel border, Middle East
raw.title: Israel–Hezbollah war elevates regional oil risk premium
raw.description: The 34-day conflict raised fears of wider regional escalation. Oil prices moved higher on the risk premium while Israeli and some Gulf equity markets experienced short-lived but sharp risk-off moves.
raw.middle_circle: Consensus expected a limited border operation; a multi-week war with measurable oil-price impact was not the base case.
raw.outer_circle: Oil and regional risk assets reacted more forcefully than typical short-security incidents before stabilising once the conflict’s containment became clearer.
raw.notes: Middle East security event with commodity spill-over. Oil and equity reaction used as proxies.

raw.title: Bank of Japan ends zero-interest-rate policy
raw.description: The Bank of Japan raised its target for the unsecured overnight call rate from effectively zero to 0.25%, ending the zero-interest-rate policy that had been in place since 2001 (and quantitative easing earlier in 2006). The official discount rate was also raised to 0.4%.
raw.middle_circle: Widely anticipated after the end of quantitative easing in March; markets expected a cautious, one-off move rather than a rapid tightening cycle.
raw.outer_circle: Yen strengthened modestly. Japanese equities were mixed. Global carry-trade dynamics adjusted as Japanese rates moved off the floor. The decision signaled confidence in Japan's exit from deflation.
sources: New York Times and Japan Times coverage
raw.notes: First rate increase by the BOJ in six years; symbolic normalization of Japanese monetary policy.

raw.title: Crude oil hits nominal record highs near $77-78 amid Middle East conflict
raw.description: WTI and Brent crude futures reached new all-time nominal highs (WTI settling near $77, Brent briefly above $78) driven by the Israel-Lebanon conflict, ongoing Iran nuclear tensions, Nigerian disruptions and the broader geopolitical risk premium.
raw.middle_circle: Analysts had expected elevated prices but the speed of the spike to new records exceeded many near-term forecasts; some warned of $80+ if the conflict widened.
raw.outer_circle: Energy equities outperformed while broader equity indexes declined on inflation and growth concerns. Retail gasoline prices in the U.S. approached or exceeded $3 per gallon. The peak proved temporary as the conflict remained contained.
raw.notes: Highest nominal oil prices of 2006; real prices remained below 1980s peaks.

raw.title: U.S. housing market shows clear signs of cooling
raw.description: By mid-to-late 2006, multiple indicators confirmed a substantial cooling of the U.S. housing market after years of rapid price appreciation. Home sales, construction and price growth decelerated markedly, with some regions experiencing outright declines.
raw.middle_circle: Many analysts had expected a soft landing or gradual slowdown; the speed of the cooling in some metrics surprised consensus and raised recession concerns.
raw.outer_circle: Homebuilder stocks underperformed. Mortgage-related securities began showing early stress. The Fed cited housing cooling as a key factor supporting the decision to pause rate hikes. Longer-term implications for the broader economy became a central market theme.
raw.notes: Early manifestation of the housing downturn that later contributed to the 2007-2008 financial crisis; exact single-day timestamp not applicable.

raw.title: BP begins shutdown of Prudhoe Bay oil field due to pipeline corrosion
raw.description: BP announced it was shutting down approximately 400,000 barrels per day of production at the Prudhoe Bay field (about 8% of U.S. crude output) after discovering severe corrosion and a small leak in transit pipelines. Full restoration was expected to take months.
raw.middle_circle: Markets had not anticipated a major U.S. domestic supply disruption of this scale; the news added to already elevated geopolitical risk premiums.
raw.outer_circle: Oil prices jumped more than $2 to settle near $77 per barrel (approaching the July record). BP shares declined. West Coast refiners faced the greatest impact. The Department of Energy indicated Strategic Petroleum Reserve releases were available if needed. Partial production was later restored faster than initially feared.
raw.notes: Largest single domestic U.S. oil-supply disruption of 2006.

raw.title: Federal Reserve pauses rate hikes, holds federal funds rate at 5.25%
raw.description: For the first time in 17 consecutive meetings, the FOMC left the target federal funds rate unchanged at 5.25%. The statement cited moderating growth (including housing cooling) and expected inflation pressures to ease, while noting that some inflation risks remained. One member (Lacker) dissented in favor of a hike.
raw.middle_circle: Markets had assigned high probability to a pause after the June statement; the decision was widely anticipated but the dissent and residual hawkish language were watched closely.
raw.outer_circle: Equities and bonds reacted positively to the confirmation of the pause. The decision marked the end of the 2004-2006 tightening cycle. Subsequent meetings through year-end also held rates steady.
raw.notes: Key turning point in the Bernanke Fed's first year.

raw.title: Israel-Lebanon ceasefire takes effect
raw.description: A United Nations-brokered ceasefire ended the 34-day conflict between Israel and Hezbollah. The cessation of major hostilities reduced the immediate geopolitical risk premium in energy markets.
raw.middle_circle: Markets expected some relief in the war premium but remained cautious given broader Middle East tensions including Iran.
raw.outer_circle: Oil prices began a sustained decline from summer peaks as the risk of wider regional conflict eased and other supply concerns moderated. The move contributed to the sharp second-half drop in crude prices.
raw.notes: Removal of a key driver of the mid-2006 oil spike.

raw.title: Amaranth Advisors discloses multi-billion-dollar natural-gas losses
raw.description: Amaranth Advisors, a multi-strategy hedge fund with peak assets of approximately $9.2 billion, informed investors of losses exceeding $3 billion (later revised higher to more than $6 billion) from concentrated natural-gas futures positions. The fund was forced to liquidate its energy book.
raw.middle_circle: Few outside counterparties fully appreciated the scale of Amaranth's concentrated positions; the speed of the collapse surprised the broader market.
raw.outer_circle: Natural-gas prices and related spreads experienced extreme volatility as the fund's positions were unwound. The episode raised concerns about hedge-fund systemic risk but did not trigger broader market contagion. Citadel and JPMorgan acquired the energy portfolio. The fund ultimately closed.
raw.notes: One of the largest hedge-fund collapses in history at the time; losses exceeded 65% of assets.

raw.title: Thai military stages coup against Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra
raw.description: The Royal Thai Army seized power in a bloodless coup while Prime Minister Thaksin was abroad, declaring martial law and suspending the constitution. The event created short-term political uncertainty in Southeast Asia.
raw.middle_circle: Markets expected limited economic disruption given Thailand's prior experience with coups and the relatively orderly nature of the takeover, but currency and equity volatility was anticipated.
raw.outer_circle: Thai baht suffered its largest one-day decline in nearly three years. The SET stock index and broader Asian equities fell. Credit-default-swap spreads on Thai debt widened sharply. The immediate market impact proved relatively contained and short-lived.
raw.notes: Short-term market impact was modest relative to the political significance.

raw.title: Federal Reserve holds federal funds rate at 5.25% (second consecutive pause)
raw.description: The FOMC left the target rate unchanged at 5.25% for the second consecutive meeting. The statement noted that inflation pressures seemed likely to moderate and that growth had slowed, while some inflation risks remained. Lacker again dissented in favor of a hike.
raw.middle_circle: Fully expected after the August pause and falling oil prices; markets increasingly priced a prolonged hold.
raw.outer_circle: Equities continued to recover from the May-June correction. Bond yields remained relatively stable. Confidence grew that the Fed had achieved a soft-landing trajectory.
raw.notes: Reinforced the end of the tightening cycle.

raw.title: OPEC announces production cuts in response to falling oil prices
raw.description: Facing a sharp decline in crude prices from summer peaks, OPEC agreed to production cuts totaling approximately 1.7 million barrels per day (announced in stages in October and December) to support the market.
raw.middle_circle: Markets expected OPEC to respond to the price drop; the size and credibility of the cuts were debated.
raw.outer_circle: Oil prices stabilized and partially recovered from November lows. The cuts helped establish a perceived floor near $60 per barrel in market psychology for a period.
raw.notes: Response to the second-half 2006 price collapse.

raw.title: North Korea conducts first nuclear test
raw.description: North Korea announced it had successfully conducted an underground nuclear weapons test. The claim was later confirmed by seismic data. The test drew immediate international condemnation and raised regional security concerns.
raw.middle_circle: Markets had anticipated the possibility of a test after prior missile launches; the actual event was expected to produce a temporary risk-off reaction concentrated in South Korean and regional assets.
raw.outer_circle: South Korean KOSPI fell as much as 3.6% intraday (closing ~2.4% lower). The won weakened and the yen briefly declined. Gold and oil saw modest safe-haven bids. U.S. markets largely shrugged off the news. The reaction proved short-lived as the risk of immediate escalation appeared limited.
sources: Al Jazeera, MarketWatch and Guardian contemporaneous coverage
raw.notes: First confirmed nuclear test by North Korea; market impact was regionally concentrated and temporary.

raw.title: Crude oil falls to year-to-date lows near $55-58
raw.description: After peaking near $77 in August, WTI crude declined sharply through the autumn, reaching lows below $56 in November amid high inventories, milder weather forecasts, reduced geopolitical risk and OPEC production adjustments.
raw.middle_circle: Many analysts had expected prices to remain elevated above $60; the speed and depth of the decline exceeded consensus forecasts.
raw.outer_circle: Energy equities underperformed. Lower oil prices eased inflation concerns and supported broader equity markets and consumer spending expectations. OPEC announced production cuts in response.
raw.notes: Oil ended 2006 near where it began after a volatile year; first annual decline since 2001.

raw.title: Record global M&A volume in 2006
raw.description: Global mergers and acquisitions activity reached record levels in 2006, surpassing the previous peak of the late-1990s technology boom, driven by private equity, corporate cash and favorable financing conditions.
raw.middle_circle: High deal volume had been anticipated given strong balance sheets and low credit spreads; the absolute scale still surprised some observers.
raw.outer_circle: Supported equity valuations and investment-banking revenues. Leveraged buyouts and cross-border deals remained prominent themes into year-end.
raw.notes: Structural market feature rather than single-day event; contributed to equity resilience.

raw.title: Federal Reserve holds federal funds rate at 5.25% (year-end meeting)
raw.description: The FOMC kept the target rate unchanged at 5.25% for the fourth consecutive meeting. The statement highlighted substantial cooling in the housing market while noting that the economy was expected to expand moderately.
raw.middle_circle: Fully anticipated; markets focused on the outlook language for 2007 and any hints of future easing.
raw.outer_circle: Equities closed the year near highs. The decision confirmed the pause and left the funds rate at the cycle peak for the remainder of 2006.
raw.notes: Final FOMC decision of 2006.

raw.location_name: New York, New York, United States
raw.title: U.S. equity markets close near multi-year or record highs
raw.description: Despite mid-year volatility, major U.S. equity indexes finished 2006 with solid gains (S&P 500 up approximately 13-16% including dividends in some measures, Dow near or at record levels). Strong corporate earnings and the end of Fed tightening supported the advance.
raw.middle_circle: Many strategists had expected more modest returns given the late stage of the cycle and housing concerns; the strength of the second-half recovery exceeded some forecasts.
raw.outer_circle: Equities demonstrated resilience to the May-June correction, geopolitical shocks and energy-price swings. The year closed on a constructive note for risk assets.
raw.notes: Broad-based equity strength despite multiple mid-year shocks.

raw.title: HSBC warns on U.S. subprime loan losses
raw.description: HSBC Holdings said it would set aside more funds to cover bad debts in its U.S. subprime lending portfolios, becoming one of the first global banks to publicly flag rising delinquencies. California lender New Century Financial separately indicated it expected a fourth-quarter 2006 loss. Spreads on non-investment-grade home-equity CDO tranches widened more than 200 basis points in the following two days.
raw.middle_circle: Consensus still treated subprime stress as contained in a small slice of U.S. housing; many analysts viewed HSBC's warning as idiosyncratic rather than systemic.
raw.outer_circle: CDO spreads jumped immediately and subprime-lender equities sold off, beginning a repricing of mortgage credit risk that would intensify through the year.
raw.notes: Exact announcement timestamp not independently verified; date is the widely cited calendar day of the HSBC statement.

raw.title: Shanghai Composite plunges 8.8%, sparking global equity sell-off
raw.description: The Shanghai Composite Index fell 8.8% on record volume after rumors of a possible capital-gains tax and tighter policy, its worst one-day drop in a decade. The shock transmitted globally: the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 416 points, its largest point decline since the first session after 9/11. Freddie Mac the same day said it would no longer buy the riskiest subprime mortgages and related securities.
raw.middle_circle: China's rally was widely seen as domestically contained speculation; most global desks did not expect a Shanghai correction to trigger a coordinated developed-market risk-off move.
raw.outer_circle: Risk assets sold off simultaneously across Asia, Europe and the U.S.; oil also weakened as growth fears rose. The episode showed how tightly global risk appetite had become linked.
raw.notes: Freddie Mac policy change is often dated Feb 27; some sources list it separately from the Shanghai crash. Time is approximate Shanghai close.

raw.title: New Century Financial files Chapter 11
raw.description: New Century Financial, then one of the largest U.S. subprime mortgage originators, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy after funding lines were pulled and loan defaults rose. The filing followed weeks of collapsing share price and marked the highest-profile failure of the early subprime wave. More than two dozen smaller subprime lenders had already failed in February–March.
raw.middle_circle: Many still expected failures to remain among monoline originators without threatening bank capital or interbank funding.
raw.outer_circle: Mortgage-lender equities and ABX indices weakened further; credit-spread widening accelerated as investors reassessed warehouse-line and securitization risk.
raw.notes: Exact filing time approximated to U.S. market hours.

raw.title: ECB raises key rate to 4.0%
raw.description: The European Central Bank raised its main refinancing rate by 25 basis points to 4.0%, continuing a tightening cycle aimed at inflation. The move came even as U.S. housing stress was already visible. Euro-area growth was still viewed as solid.
raw.middle_circle: Markets widely expected the hike; debate focused on how many further increases would follow rather than on credit-market contagion.
raw.outer_circle: The euro firmed and rate-hike pricing in EUR forwards held; the decision later looked mistimed as the August liquidity freeze hit euro-area banks.
raw.notes: Announcement time is the standard ECB press-conference window; exact second not verified.

raw.title: Bear Stearns hedge funds disclose large subprime losses
raw.description: Two Bear Stearns-managed hedge funds that had bet heavily on subprime-backed CDOs announced double-digit losses and began selling assets to meet redemptions and margin calls. The funds later required a multi-billion-dollar rescue and were liquidated in July. The episode was the first major Wall Street hedge-fund failure of the crisis.
raw.middle_circle: Street consensus still assumed prime brokerages could contain fund-level losses; few priced a full liquidation of high-grade CDO inventories.
raw.outer_circle: Forced selling pressured CDO and ABS prices; counterparties tightened margin, a preview of the August wholesale-funding freeze.
raw.notes: Public disclosure clustered around June 20; liquidation completed July 31.

raw.title: Rating agencies begin mass downgrades of subprime RMBS and CDOs
raw.description: Moody's and other agencies placed large numbers of mortgage-backed CDO tranches on review and began downgrades that continued through mid-July. The reviews covered hundreds of structures and signaled that AAA ratings on packaged subprime debt were no longer reliable. Subsequent waves in October covered thousands more bonds.
raw.middle_circle: Investors had treated agency ratings as sufficient due diligence; many mandates required holding only investment-grade paper.
raw.outer_circle: Forced selling by ratings-constrained holders accelerated; ABX and related credit indices gapped wider and liquidity in structured credit deteriorated.
raw.notes: BIS dates a notable Moody's review of 184 CDO tranches to 11 July; process began in early July.

raw.title: Bear Stearns funds reported nearly worthless
raw.description: Bear Stearns told investors that assets in its High-Grade Structured Credit Strategies Enhanced Leverage Fund were essentially worthless and that the companion fund had lost most of its value. The admission confirmed that even supposedly senior CDO exposure could go to zero. Liquidation of the funds was completed later in July.
raw.middle_circle: After the June margin-call news, some still hoped residual NAV would be material.
raw.outer_circle: Bear shares and broker-dealer credit spreads weakened; confidence in mark-to-model valuations of structured credit fell sharply.
raw.notes: NYT report dated July 17.

raw.title: Dow Jones Industrial Average closes above 14,000 for first time
raw.description: The Dow closed above the 14,000 level for the first time, extending a bull market that many still treated as intact despite mounting subprime losses. The print became the last major psychological high before the August credit freeze. A slightly higher close of 14,164.53 followed on October 9.
raw.middle_circle: Equity bulls argued housing stress was isolated and that global growth plus buybacks would keep indexes rising.
raw.outer_circle: The breakout proved short-lived as credit-market stress intensified within weeks; the October 9 peak marked the cycle high.
raw.notes: July 19 is the first close above 14,000; October 9 is the all-time high for the cycle.

raw.title: IKB Deutsche Industriebank rescued after ABCP freeze
raw.description: German mid-sized lender IKB, majority-owned via KfW, could not roll asset-backed commercial paper used to fund U.S. structured-credit vehicles and required an emergency rescue. Commerzbank, Deutsche Bank and KfW arranged an initial €3.5 billion support package later increased. The case showed European banks' off-balance-sheet conduits were exposed to U.S. subprime.
raw.middle_circle: European banks were widely assumed to have limited direct subprime books; conduit and SIV risk was under-appreciated.
raw.outer_circle: German and European bank shares sold off; ABCP markets seized further and Sachsen LB later needed support.
raw.notes: Rescue terms evolved over subsequent days.

raw.title: American Home Mortgage files for bankruptcy
raw.description: American Home Mortgage Investment, a large originator focused on adjustable-rate and Alt-A loans, filed for Chapter 11 after the securitization and warehouse-funding markets closed. One of its ABCP conduits extended maturities, highlighting the freeze in short-term mortgage paper. The failure added to a cascade of originator collapses.
raw.middle_circle: Alt-A lenders were thought safer than pure subprime shops; many expected GSEs and banks to absorb the origination slack.
raw.outer_circle: ABCP spreads blew out and more conduits invoked extendible features; mortgage-originator equity was effectively wiped out across the sector.
raw.notes: Location is AHM headquarters area.

raw.title: BNP Paribas freezes three ABS funds; ECB injects €95bn
raw.description: BNP Paribas suspended NAV calculation and redemptions on three ABS funds worth about €1.6 billion, saying U.S. securitization liquidity had 'completely evaporated' so assets could not be valued. The ECB the same day allotted €94.8 billion in a special fine-tuning operation, its largest such injection since 9/11. The episode is widely treated as the start of the global credit crunch.
raw.middle_circle: Markets expected sporadic fund gates but not a major universal bank to declare structured-credit markets unpriceable, nor an ECB operation of that size.
raw.outer_circle: Interbank spreads exploded, LIBOR-OIS widened, equity volatility jumped and risk assets sold off globally. Northern Rock later called it 'the day the world changed'.
raw.notes: BNP statement and ECB operation occurred the same calendar day; exact intra-day sequencing varies by source.

raw.title: Federal Reserve injects emergency liquidity after credit freeze
raw.description: Following the BNP/ECB shock, the Federal Reserve added tens of billions of dollars via open-market operations as U.S. funding markets seized. Other major central banks also injected cash. The coordinated response signaled that the disruption was global rather than a euro-area technical issue.
raw.middle_circle: Many expected a one-day ECB operation to calm Europe without a comparable U.S. funding squeeze.
raw.outer_circle: U.S. commercial-paper and repo markets remained impaired; equity volatility stayed elevated into the following week.
raw.notes: Fed also held an August 10 conference call; precise allotment figures vary by operation.

raw.title: Countrywide draws $11.5bn credit line; rating cuts hit ResCap
raw.description: Countrywide Financial, the largest U.S. mortgage lender, drew its entire $11.5 billion backup credit line after commercial-paper markets closed to it. Fitch and Moody's cut ratings on Countrywide and GMAC's ResCap unit. Shares plunged and depositors queued at Countrywide Bank branches the next day.
raw.middle_circle: Countrywide had insisted it had ample liquidity and would gain share as rivals failed; bankruptcy talk was viewed as alarmist.
raw.outer_circle: CFC stock suffered one of its worst days since 1987; bank and homebuilder shares sold off and mortgage-credit availability tightened further.
raw.notes: Rating actions and the credit-line draw clustered on Aug 16; depositor run visible Aug 17.

raw.title: Fed cuts discount rate 50bp in inter-meeting surprise
raw.description: The Federal Reserve Board cut the primary credit (discount) rate by 50 basis points to 5.75% and issued a statement that downside risks to growth from tightening credit markets had increased 'appreciably'. The funds-rate target was left at 5.25%. It was the first easing signal after a long tightening cycle.
raw.middle_circle: Most expected no inter-meeting action this soon after the August freeze; a discount-rate-only move was not fully priced.
raw.outer_circle: World equities rallied sharply from multi-month lows; financials outperformed on the day as traders priced a coming funds-rate cut.
raw.notes: Typical FOMC-style release window used for timestamp.

raw.location_name: Newcastle upon Tyne / London, United Kingdom
raw.title: Northern Rock bank run and Bank of England liquidity support
raw.description: After wholesale funding markets froze, Northern Rock sought emergency liquidity from the Bank of England. The announcement triggered the first major UK retail bank run since the 19th century, with £4.6bn withdrawn in days and queues outside branches.
raw.middle_circle: Consensus viewed Northern Rock’s mortgage-book risks as manageable and expected orderly private resolution; a full retail run was considered improbable in a modern deposit-insurance regime.
raw.outer_circle: Share price halved, CDS spreads exploded, and contagion hit other UK lenders; the government was forced to guarantee all deposits within days—far more interventionist than pre-announcement pricing implied.
raw.notes: Classic UK-specific catalyst under-weighted versus US subprime narrative. Deposit-flow and share-volume data used as proxy.

raw.title: Northern Rock receives Bank of England emergency facility; retail run begins
raw.description: The BBC and company announcements revealed that Northern Rock had obtained a Bank of England lender-of-last-resort facility after wholesale markets closed to it. Shares fell more than 30% and retail depositors queued at branches over subsequent days, withdrawing about £4.6 billion (roughly 20% of retail deposits) in four days. It was the first major British bank run in more than a century.
raw.middle_circle: Authorities hoped announcing official liquidity support would reassure markets; few expected a televised retail run.
raw.outer_circle: The announcement confirmed distress and triggered the run. Peer mortgage-bank shares and CDS widened; sterling funding markets stressed.
raw.notes: News broke late on Sep 13 UK time / early Sep 14; run visible Sep 14–17.

raw.title: UK authorities guarantee Northern Rock deposits
raw.description: After a weekend of queues, Chancellor Alistair Darling announced that existing Northern Rock deposits would be guaranteed during the instability. The move was designed to stop the retail run and limit contagion to other UK mortgage banks. The Bank of England also broadened term liquidity against a wider collateral set.
raw.middle_circle: Markets expected some form of political reassurance but not an open-ended deposit guarantee this early.
raw.outer_circle: Queues receded after the guarantee; bank-sector CDS remained elevated and UK housing and mortgage-credit expectations deteriorated.
raw.notes: Guarantee statements spanned Sep 17; nationalization followed in February 2008.

raw.title: Fed cuts federal funds rate 50bp to 4.75%
raw.description: In its first funds-rate cut since 2003, the FOMC reduced the target by an unusually large 50 basis points to 4.75% and cut the discount rate by the same amount. The statement framed the move as insurance against credit-market damage to the real economy. It was a sharp reversal from the inflation-focused stance of earlier 2007 meetings.
raw.middle_circle: A 25bp cut was widely expected; a 50bp 'shock therapy' move was only a minority view.
raw.outer_circle: The Dow jumped about 336 points (2.5%) on the day. Financials and high-beta equities led; the dollar weakened and Treasuries mixed as growth-insurance was priced in.
raw.notes: Standard 2:15 p.m. ET FOMC release window.

raw.title: Dow Jones hits cycle all-time high of 14,164
raw.description: The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at 14,164.53, the peak of the 2002–2007 bull market. The high came even as bank write-down announcements were accelerating. The index would not regain that level until 2013.
raw.middle_circle: Many strategists still expected the Fed easing cycle to extend the equity bull market into 2008.
raw.outer_circle: The high marked exhaustion: financials were already rolling over and credit conditions kept tightening beneath a still-elevated index level.
raw.notes: Close value commonly cited as 14,164.53.

raw.title: Citigroup reports 57% drop in Q3 profit on write-downs
raw.description: Citigroup posted a 57% decline in third-quarter profit, including about $6.5 billion of write-downs and losses tied to subprime and fixed-income markets. CEO Charles Prince called the result 'frankly surprising'. The print confirmed that the largest U.S. bank by assets was deeply exposed.
raw.middle_circle: Analysts expected weaker trading results but underestimated the scale of super-senior and warehouse losses still to come.
raw.outer_circle: Citi shares extended their decline; bank-sector multiples compressed and funding-spread pressure on large U.S. banks increased.
raw.notes: Earnings release morning U.S. time.

raw.title: Merrill Lynch posts large write-down; oil pushes toward $90
raw.description: Merrill Lynch reported a quarterly loss driven by multi-billion-dollar write-downs on CDOs and subprime-related assets, one of the first bulge-bracket prints to show the damage inside investment banks. In the same week WTI crude closed above $90 as Middle East tensions, inventory draws and a weak dollar combined. Equity and credit markets digested both inflation and bank-capital shocks at once.
raw.middle_circle: Write-down estimates for Merrill had been rising but still lagged the eventual total; $90 oil was treated as a psychological but not yet recessionary threshold.
raw.outer_circle: Broker-dealer stocks fell; energy outperformed. Cross-asset vol rose as growth and inflation risks were priced simultaneously.
raw.notes: Merrill earnings and the $90 oil close are clustered in late October; WTI first settled above $90 on Oct 25–26.

raw.title: Fed cuts funds rate 25bp to 4.50%
raw.description: The FOMC lowered the federal funds target by 25 basis points to 4.50% and the discount rate to 5.00%. Officials described inflation and growth risks as roughly balanced. Markets had largely expected the quarter-point move.
raw.middle_circle: A 25bp cut was consensus; some wanted another 50bp after the September surprise.
raw.outer_circle: Stocks initially rose then faded as the balanced-risk language was read as less dovish than hoped. Credit conditions did not ease materially.
raw.notes: Standard FOMC release time.

raw.title: Citigroup CEO Charles Prince resigns; $8–11bn additional write-down
raw.description: Citigroup announced that Chairman and CEO Charles Prince had retired and that it expected an additional $8–11 billion pre-tax reduction in the fair value of subprime-related exposures. Robert Rubin became chairman and Win Bischoff acting CEO. The disclosure dwarfed the third-quarter charge and raised questions about capital and the dividend.
raw.middle_circle: Prince's job was already in doubt after Q3, but the size of the incremental write-down exceeded most published estimates that weekend.
raw.outer_circle: Citi and bank stocks fell when markets reopened; credit-default swaps on large U.S. banks widened and financial-sector funding stress returned.
raw.notes: Announcement Sunday Nov 4; price action Nov 5.

raw.title: WTI crude settles at record near $97 on supply-risk headlines
raw.description: Front-month WTI rose to a then-record settlement near $96.70 after attacks on energy infrastructure in Yemen, bombings in Afghanistan, North Sea weather risk and expectations of another U.S. inventory draw. Geopolitical premia around Iran and northern Iraq remained elevated. Oil was up roughly two-thirds year-to-date.
raw.middle_circle: Demand-driven tightness was widely accepted; the speed of the final $75-to-$97 run was still debated as partly speculative.
raw.outer_circle: Energy equities outperformed; rate-cut hopes and a weak dollar amplified the move. Growth-sensitive equities struggled under the inflation impulse.
raw.notes: Intraday high above $97; settlement slightly lower.

raw.title: Oil trades above $99; global stocks slump, 10-year yield under 4%
raw.description: Crude traded through $99 a barrel while Fed commentary pointed to a deeper U.S. slowdown. Asian and European equities fell and U.S. 10-year yields dropped below 4% for the first time since 2005 as investors fled to Treasuries. The euro printed a then-record near $1.49.
raw.middle_circle: $100 oil had been treated as a 2008 event; simultaneous growth scare plus inflation scare was not the base case.
raw.outer_circle: Risk-off across equities and credit; curve bull-flattened and the dollar weakened on rate-cut expectations.
raw.notes: Price action spanned Nov 20–21 across time zones.

raw.title: NBER later dates U.S. recession as beginning December 2007
raw.description: The National Bureau of Economic Research subsequently determined that the U.S. expansion peaked in December 2007, marking the start of the Great Recession. At the time unemployment was about 5% and household net worth near a cycle high. Real-time GDP was not yet printing consecutive declines.
raw.middle_circle: In real time most forecasters still called for a slowdown or mild downturn, not an 18-month recession.
raw.outer_circle: Equity markets had not priced a recession start in December; the official dating is retrospective and was announced in 2008.
raw.notes: Not a contemporaneous announcement. Included because it is the official cycle peak used by market historians. Date-time set to month start; location is Washington as NBER reference.

raw.title: U.S. NIE says Iran halted nuclear-weapons work in 2003
raw.description: A declassified National Intelligence Estimate concluded that Iran had halted its nuclear weapons program in 2003, reducing perceived odds of an imminent U.S. or Israeli strike. Oil prices fell as part of the geopolitical premium unwound, though President Bush argued Iran remained dangerous. OPEC meeting speculation added to the two-way tape.
raw.middle_circle: A sizable war-risk premium had been embedded in crude on fears of Strait of Hormuz disruption.
raw.outer_circle: WTI dropped nearly $1 on the session and remained under pressure into the OPEC meeting; the geopolitical bid in oil faded for several weeks.
raw.notes: NIE release dated early December 2007; oil reaction visible Dec 3–4.

raw.title: Fed cuts 25bp to 4.25%; stocks sell off on cautious statement
raw.description: The FOMC cut the funds rate 25 basis points to 4.25% and the discount rate to 4.75%, the third consecutive meeting cut. The statement declined to say whether growth or inflation was the greater concern and highlighted rising uncertainty from financial conditions. Investors who wanted a stronger easing signal sold equities.
raw.middle_circle: A 25bp cut was expected; a sizable camp wanted 50bp and more explicit growth-risk language.
raw.outer_circle: The Dow dropped about 294 points (2.1%) after the release; Treasuries rallied. The reaction showed markets now demanded more than mechanical quarter-point cuts.
raw.notes: Standard FOMC release time.

raw.title: Fed announces Term Auction Facility with other central banks
raw.description: The Federal Reserve announced the Term Auction Facility to auction term funds to depository institutions against a wide collateral set, aiming to relieve stigma in discount-window borrowing. Coordinated actions with the ECB, SNB and Bank of England provided dollar liquidity abroad. TAF became a core crisis tool into 2008.
raw.middle_circle: After the disappointing Dec 11 cut, markets wanted a concrete funding facility; details and take-up were uncertain.
raw.outer_circle: LIBOR-OIS and term funding spreads eased modestly on the announcement but did not normalize; bank stocks stabilized only briefly.
raw.notes: Announcement followed the Dec 11 FOMC; first auctions occurred later in December.

raw.title: Bank of America agrees to buy Countrywide for about $4 billion
raw.description: Bank of America announced an all-stock deal valued at about $4 billion to acquire Countrywide Financial, the largest U.S. mortgage originator, which had been locked out of wholesale funding markets since August 2007. The price was a fraction of Countrywide's 2007 peak valuation. The deal concentrated U.S. mortgage origination further inside a commercial bank and marked the end of the independent monoline-lender model.
raw.middle_circle: Many expected Countrywide to fail or require a government-assisted resolution; a clean strategic bid from BofA at any price was not consensus.
raw.outer_circle: Countrywide stock jumped on the bid while BofA shares sold off on dilution and credit-risk concerns. Mortgage-lender CDS tightened modestly on the hope that a large bank would backstop origination.
raw.notes: Deal announced Jan 11; closed later in 2008. Timestamp approximated to U.S. morning announcement.

raw.title: Citigroup reports $18.1 billion fourth-quarter loss
raw.description: Citigroup posted an $18.1 billion fourth-quarter 2007 loss driven by write-downs on subprime CDOs and other credit assets, one of the largest quarterly losses in U.S. banking history at the time. Merrill Lynch reported an $11.5 billion quarterly loss two days later. The prints confirmed that 2007 charges had not cleared the books.
raw.middle_circle: Street estimates had risen through January but still understated the CDO and super-senior marks.
raw.outer_circle: Bank stocks and the XLF sold off; funding spreads for large U.S. banks remained elevated into the late-January equity slump.
raw.notes: Citi print Jan 15; Merrill Jan 17. Combined as the mid-January bank-earnings shock.

raw.title: European equities crash as SocGen unwinds Kerviel futures book
raw.description: European indexes suffered their worst session since 9/11, with the DAX down about 7.2% and the FTSEurofirst 300 off nearly 6%. Société Générale was secretly unwinding tens of billions of euros of unauthorized long equity-index futures built by trader Jérôme Kerviel. U.S. markets were closed for Martin Luther King Day, so the shock hit Asia and Europe first.
raw.middle_circle: The sell-off was initially attributed solely to U.S. recession fears after a weak January; almost no one knew a large bank was liquidating a hidden futures book.
raw.outer_circle: DAX and Euro Stoxx futures volume exploded. The rout helped trigger the Fed's inter-meeting 75bp cut the next day when U.S. markets reopened.
raw.notes: SocGen later said it discovered the positions Jan 18–20 and began closing them Jan 21. Causal weight versus macro news remains debated.

raw.title: Fed emergency cut of 75bp to 3.50%, largest in 23 years
raw.description: In a rare inter-meeting action, the FOMC slashed the federal funds target by 75 basis points to 3.50% after a global equity rout and rising recession risk. It was the largest single cut since 1984. The statement cited a weakening outlook and increasing downside risks to growth.
raw.middle_circle: Futures had priced some easing at the Jan 29–30 meeting, not a 75bp surprise while U.S. cash equities were closed the prior session.
raw.outer_circle: U.S. stocks opened lower but recovered much of the European damage. The move reset the easing path for the rest of Q1.
raw.notes: Conference-call decision Jan 21 evening U.S. time; announcement Jan 22.

raw.title: Société Générale discloses €4.9 billion rogue-trader loss
raw.description: Société Générale announced that unauthorized equity-index futures trades by Jérôme Kerviel had produced a €4.9 billion ($7.2 billion) loss, then the largest single-trader loss on record. The bank said it would raise €5.5 billion of capital. Positions had been closed into the Jan 21–22 crash.
raw.middle_circle: Markets knew European banks had subprime marks coming; a multi-billion operational-risk loss of this size was not in anyone's base case.
raw.outer_circle: SocGen shares plunged. The disclosure retroactively explained part of Monday's European volume spike and kept bank-sector risk premia elevated.
raw.notes: Public announcement Jan 24 after markets had already absorbed the unwind.

raw.title: Fed cuts funds rate another 50bp to 3.00%
raw.description: At its scheduled meeting the FOMC cut the funds rate a further 50 basis points to 3.00%, bringing January easing to 125bp. Officials still noted inflation risks even as they responded to deteriorating financial conditions.
raw.middle_circle: After the 75bp surprise, another 50bp was widely expected; debate was whether the Fed would pause.
raw.outer_circle: Equities initially firmed then faded. The path toward 2% by spring was now the working assumption.
raw.notes: Standard 2:15 p.m. ET release window.

raw.title: Bush signs Economic Stimulus Act of 2008
raw.description: President George W. Bush signed a fiscal package providing tax rebates to households and bonus depreciation for business investment. Checks began arriving in the spring. It was the first major fiscal response to the emerging recession.
raw.middle_circle: Markets expected a rebate-centered bill after bipartisan talks; size was roughly in line with forecasts.
raw.outer_circle: Limited immediate price action. Later data showed rebates lifted Q2 consumption temporarily without reversing the housing-credit shock.
raw.notes: Lower market-impact score than banking events; included as the year's first large fiscal catalyst.

raw.title: UK nationalizes Northern Rock
raw.description: The British government announced the temporary nationalization of Northern Rock after private-sale talks failed. The lender had been on Bank of England life support since September 2007. Taxpayers assumed the funding and the mortgage book.
raw.middle_circle: A private bid from Virgin or others was still considered possible; full nationalization was the downside scenario.
raw.outer_circle: UK bank shares weakened on nationalization-risk repricing. Gilt and sterling reaction was contained relative to later 2008 UK rescues.
raw.notes: Announcement Feb 17, 2008.

raw.title: Fed launches Term Securities Lending Facility (TSLF)
raw.description: The Federal Reserve announced the TSLF, allowing primary dealers to swap less-liquid mortgage securities for Treasuries. It was a direct attempt to unfreeze dealer balance sheets before a full run on a broker-dealer. The facility went live later in March.
raw.middle_circle: Dealers wanted a Treasury-for-MBS swap; few expected the Fed to extend lender-of-last-resort support this far beyond banks so quickly.
raw.outer_circle: Agency MBS and dealer-broker stocks bounced briefly. The relief lasted only days before Bear Stearns' liquidity run accelerated.
raw.notes: Announcement March 11; Bear run peaked March 13–16.

raw.title: Fed and JPMorgan provide emergency financing to Bear Stearns
raw.description: After a prime-brokerage and short-term funding run, Bear Stearns received emergency financing through JPMorgan backed by the New York Fed, the first such broker rescue since the 1930s. Shares fell 46% to $30.85. Rating downgrades and client withdrawals left the firm facing insolvency before Asia opened Sunday.
raw.middle_circle: Bear had insisted its balance sheet was sound earlier in the week; a Fed-backed lifeline in mid-session was a shock.
raw.outer_circle: Financials dumped. The print told markets that even a large independent investment bank could lose access to funding in days.
raw.notes: Facility announced Friday March 14; sale negotiated over the weekend.

raw.title: JPMorgan agrees to buy Bear Stearns for $2 a share; Fed opens PDCF
raw.description: JPMorgan announced it would acquire Bear Stearns for about $2 a share, later raised to $10, with the New York Fed financing up to $30 billion of less-liquid Bear assets via Maiden Lane. The Fed also created the Primary Dealer Credit Facility and cut the discount rate. An 85-year-old partnership was extinguished over a weekend.
raw.middle_circle: A higher rescue price or a standalone recap had still been hoped for on Friday. $2/share implied near-total equity wipeout.
raw.outer_circle: Bear stock collapsed toward the bid. Other broker-dealers' CDS blew out as moral-hazard and funding-risk premia jumped. Equities sold off into the March 17 open.
raw.notes: Deal announced Sunday evening March 16 U.S. time. Fed later revised support figures; initial press cited about $30bn.

raw.title: Fed cuts funds rate 75bp to 2.25% after Bear weekend
raw.description: The FOMC cut the federal funds target by 75 basis points to 2.25%, the lowest since 2005. The move followed the Bear Stearns rescue and aimed to cushion the real economy from a funding shock. Inflation concerns were still present in the statement.
raw.middle_circle: A 50–75bp cut was expected after the weekend; 75bp was the dovish end of the range.
raw.outer_circle: Stocks rallied hard on the cut. Financials bounced from deeply oversold levels even as credit spreads stayed wide.
raw.notes: Scheduled March 18 meeting.

raw.title: Fed cuts 25bp to 2.00% and signals a possible pause
raw.description: The FOMC trimmed the funds rate 25 basis points to 2.00%, completing 325bp of cuts since September 2007. Language suggested the Committee might pause to watch incoming data and inflation. Risk assets treated 2% as a near-term floor until autumn.
raw.middle_circle: A 25bp cut was consensus; markets wanted confirmation that emergency easing was ending.
raw.outer_circle: Equities were mixed. Oil and other commodities remained well bid into early summer as dollar weakness and demand narratives dominated.
raw.notes: Last cut until the October emergency coordinated move.

raw.title: Sichuan earthquake kills tens of thousands
raw.description: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck Wenchuan County, killing nearly 70,000 people and devastating infrastructure in a major Chinese industrial and agricultural province. Reconstruction demand and supply disruptions affected regional metals and construction. Global risk sentiment wobbled alongside already-elevated commodity prices.
raw.middle_circle: Markets did not immediately treat the quake as a global growth shock; China was still viewed as structurally strong.
raw.outer_circle: Shanghai stocks fell then recovered on reconstruction hopes. Industrial metals were two-way as supply damage offset demand fears.
raw.notes: Origin time 06:28 UTC May 12. Included as the year's largest natural-disaster catalyst with measurable China-market impact.

raw.title: WTI hits all-time high $147.27; IndyMac seized
raw.description: Front-month WTI traded to an intraday record of $147.27 a barrel on Iran-war premia, Nigerian and other supply outages, and a weak dollar. The same day U.S. regulators seized IndyMac Bank, then the largest regulated-thrift failure. The juxtaposition of record oil and a retail-bank run captured mid-2008's split macro regime.
raw.middle_circle: Goldman and others still discussed a path toward $150–$200 oil; IndyMac stress had been visible after a senator's public warning but seizure timing was not precisely timed.
raw.outer_circle: Energy led commodities to cycle highs. Financials sold off on the thrift failure. Within days oil began a collapse that would take WTI below $40 by year-end.
raw.notes: Intraday high July 11; some series cite July 3 close near $145. IndyMac closed July 11.

raw.title: SEC temporarily bans naked short sales in major financials
raw.description: The SEC issued an emergency order restricting naked short selling in Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and 17 other large financial stocks. Treasury and Fed had just extended support to the GSEs. The ban was an attempt to stop what officials called abusive bear raids.
raw.middle_circle: A GSE backstop was expected after the July 13 Treasury/Fed statements; a short-sale ban was more controversial.
raw.outer_circle: GSE and bank stocks squeezed higher short-term. The relief faded as capital questions at Fannie and Freddie persisted into September.
raw.notes: Emergency order July 15, 2008.

raw.title: Bush signs Housing and Economic Recovery Act
raw.description: HERA created the Federal Housing Finance Agency, authorized Treasury to purchase GSE obligations, and expanded foreclosure-relief tools. It was the statutory foundation for the September conservatorships of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.
raw.middle_circle: Markets had priced a GSE backstop after mid-July statements; the signed law removed residual legislative risk.
raw.outer_circle: Agency spreads tightened on the backstop language. Equity in the GSEs remained under pressure because conservatorship risk was still live.
raw.notes: Public Law 110-289 signed July 30.

raw.title: Russo-Georgian war begins
raw.description: Georgia moved forces into South Ossetia; Russia launched a full-scale intervention, advancing toward Gori and threatening Tbilisi. Fighting lasted days until a French-brokered ceasefire. Russian equities and the ruble sold off sharply and capital fled, compounding later global-crisis losses.
raw.middle_circle: A limited South Ossetia clash was possible after months of incidents; a Russian advance into Georgia proper was the tail risk.
raw.outer_circle: Russia's finance minister said $6 billion of value was lost on Aug 8 alone. RTS later became one of 2008's worst major indexes. Oil was two-way on Caucasus-supply risk versus global-growth fear.
raw.notes: Combat intensified Aug 7–8 local time. Coordinates use Tskhinvali as the initial flashpoint.

raw.title: FHFA places Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac into conservatorship
raw.description: The U.S. government seized Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, replacing management and pledging capital to firms that guaranteed a large share of U.S. mortgages. Treasury took preferred stock and warrants. It was Washington's most dramatic credit-crisis intervention to that date.
raw.middle_circle: A support package was expected; full conservatorship wiping common and preferred equity surprised many preferred holders, including banks.
raw.outer_circle: GSE common and preferred collapsed. Agency MBS and Treasury yields fell on the explicit backstop. Some banks took immediate preferred-stock losses.
raw.notes: Announcement Sunday Sep 7.

raw.title: Lehman Brothers files largest U.S. bankruptcy; BofA buys Merrill
raw.description: Lehman Brothers Holdings filed Chapter 11 with about $600 billion of assets after Treasury refused a Bear-style rescue and Barclays could not close a deal. The same morning Bank of America agreed to buy Merrill Lynch for about $50 billion in stock. Counterparties, money funds and swap markets seized.
raw.middle_circle: Over the weekend many still expected a sale or public backstop; allowing a top-five investment bank to fail was the moral-hazard experiment.
raw.outer_circle: The Dow fell 504 points. Interbank and CP markets froze. Reserve Primary later broke the buck on Lehman paper. Global risk assets entered a crash phase.
raw.notes: Filings and deal announcements pre-U.S. open Sep 15.

raw.title: Russian equities crash in global financial crisis peak
raw.description: As Lehman failed and global risk appetite collapsed, the RTS and MICEX indices suffered extreme losses. Russia’s heavy commodity dependence and leveraged local banks amplified the external shock, producing one of the sharpest emerging-market equity drawdowns of the period.
raw.middle_circle: Consensus still viewed Russia’s large reserves and fiscal surplus as buffers that would limit the equity and FX impact relative to other emerging markets.
raw.outer_circle: Equity indices fell far more than most peer markets, the ruble came under pressure, and capital outflows accelerated beyond the soft-landing assumptions that had dominated mid-2008 forecasts.
raw.notes: Russia amplification of global crisis via commodity and banking channels. Equity volume used as proxy.

raw.title: Lehman Brothers files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy
raw.description: After failed weekend negotiations for a sale or rescue, Lehman Brothers Holdings filed the largest bankruptcy in US history (~$639bn assets). The failure crystallised counterparty risk fears across global markets.
raw.middle_circle: Many expected a government-brokered sale or backstop similar to Bear Stearns; outright failure of a primary dealer was viewed as too systemically dangerous.
raw.outer_circle: Dow fell >500 points (~4.4%), credit spreads gapped wider by tens of basis points in a day, money-market funds broke the buck, and interbank markets seized—far exceeding the orderly-resolution scenarios priced the prior Friday.
raw.notes: Central US event. CDS notional and equity volume on the day used as strongest available proxies.
